notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on 1 Chronicles 8, drawn from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Overview of the Chapter

This chapter returns to the tribe of Benjamin, which was briefly treated in 1 Chronicles 7:6–12. The Chronicler revisits Benjamin **mainly to introduce the lineage of Saul**, Israel's first king, who was of this tribe. The genealogy of Benjamin thus serves as the "perch" from which the narrative history (beginning in ch. 10 with Saul's death) will be launched. Additionally, Benjamin was the only tribe other than Judah to remain loyal to the Davidic line and to return in significant numbers from the Babylonian exile. (Pulpit Commentary, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm); Constable, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-8.html))

The chapter falls into two major sections: (a) the sons and chief men of Benjamin generally (vv. 1–28), and (b) the family of Gibeon, especially the royal house of Saul (vv. 29–40). (Poole, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/1-chronicles-8.html))

---

## Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1: "Benjamin was the father of Bela, his firstborn; Ashbel was the second born, Aharah the third"

- The genealogy of Benjamin is revisited more fully here than in ch. 7, partly for Saul's sake and partly because Benjamin went with Judah into Babylon and returned in relatively large numbers. (Poole, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/1-chronicles-8.html))
- Gill notes that this review is "chiefly for the sake of Saul, and his posterity, the first king of Israel." (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Bela**: The same as the Bela of Numbers 26:38. **Ashbel** is "supposed to be the same with Jediael" of 1 Chronicles 7:6. **Aharah** corresponds to Ahiram (Numbers 26:38) and to Aher of 1 Chronicles 7:13. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- Ellicott notes that this list (five sons) agrees with Numbers 26:38 in assigning five sons to Benjamin, and aligns better with the Pentateuch data than the list in 1 Chronicles 7. (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- The Pulpit Commentary observes that Becher (1 Chr 7:6) does not appear here; Ashbel appears in his place. The Hebrew word for "firstborn" in Genesis 46:21 may, by an ancient scribal error, have been turned into the proper name Becher. (Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### v. 2: "Nohah the fourth, and Rapha the fifth."

- **Nohah** and **Rapha** are names not found in the other Benjamin lists (Genesis 46; Numbers 26). Nohah is "supposed by some to be the same with Becher" (1 Chr 7:6). Rapha may be the same as Rosh in Genesis 46:21. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- Ellicott suggests Nohah and Rapha "represent different clans, which were prominent at the time when the present list was draughted." Rapha reminds us of the Valley of Rephaim, south-west of Jerusalem (1 Chr 11:15). (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- The Pulpit Commentary says nothing is known of these two elsewhere, though it may be possible to count five families from Numbers 26:38–39. (Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### vv. 3–5: The nine sons of Bela

- **Nine sons** are assigned to Bela. Only three are clearly found in Genesis 46:21 (Gera, Naaman, and Ard), and three in Numbers 26:39–40 (Ard, Naaman, and Shupham). The names Shephuphan and Huram here may correspond to Shupham and Hupham (Numbers 26:39), and to Muppim and Huppim (Genesis 46:21). (Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Addar** is the same as Ard (Numbers 26:40). **Gera** appears as brother of Bela in Genesis 46:21, yet here appears as a son of Bela — illustrating the vagueness of kinship terms in clan genealogies. (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- The repetition of **Gera** in v. 5 so soon after v. 3 may reflect textual disorder, or may indicate that there were two great Benjamite houses bearing that name. (Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm); Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Naaman** appears as a son of Bela in Numbers 26:40 and as a brother in Genesis 46:21. The family of the Naamanites descended from this grandson. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### vv. 6–7: The descendants of Ehud and the exile to Manahath

- **Ehud**: Not the judge Ehud of Judges 3:15, though the Hebrew spelling is nearly identical. Gill suggests he may have been a son of Huram (v. 5). Some identify him with Abihud (v. 3) or Ahoah (v. 4). (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm); Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- These descendants were **heads of families living in Geba** (a Benjamite city, Joshua 18:24). They were **exiled/removed to Manahath**. The Hebrew verb can mean "carried them captive" or "transported them." (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Gera** seems to have been the chief promoter or leader of this removal. After the removal, he (or Ehud) fathered Uzza and Ahihud in Manahath. (Poole, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/1-chronicles-8.html))
- Ellicott renders: *"These are the sons of Ehud. (These are heads of clans belonging to the inhabitants of Geba, and men carried them away to Manahath — both Naaman, and Ahijah, and Gera, he it was who carried them away.) He begat Uzza and Ahihud."* (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- Poole notes the genealogies of Benjamin were "broken by that almost total extirpation of this tribe, Judges 20," accounting for the fragmentary nature of the record. (Poole, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/1-chronicles-8.html))

### v. 8: "Shaharaim had sons in the country of Moab after he had divorced his wives Hushim and Baara."

- **Shaharaim**: He appears "out of all connection" with the other Benjamite houses. Possibly a son or brother of Ahihud, or another son of Ehud. Expelled from Geba, he found refuge in Moab (cf. Elimelech in Ruth 1; David in 1 Sam 22:3–4). (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm); Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- The Hebrew text is "certainly corrupt" according to Ellicott. The easiest correction reads "after divorcing Hushim and Baara his wives" rather than the Masoretic "after he had sent them away." (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- The Pulpit Commentary agrees a copyist's error gave "them" (אֹתָם) instead of the direct object marker (אֶת) before the wives' names. The sentence would thus translate: "after his sending away [whether by divorce or not] Hushim and Baara his wives." (Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary notes that some think Hodesh (v. 9) is another name for Baara, "so called because her husband, after long desertion, returned in affection to her." Others see Shaharaim as a polygamist who divorced two wives — a "brand upon him" for lack of natural affection. (Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-chronicles-8.html))
- **Pulpit Homiletics** draws a moral lesson: "Alliances often end in entanglements and entail unconsidered consequences." Shaharaim went into Moab, married there, and the names of his sons (Mesha, Malcham) have Moabitish associations — Malcham being the name of a Moabite/Ammonite idol. "If we 'make affinity' with those who are not of like mind and like principles with ourselves, we must be prepared for serious spiritual consequences." (Pulpit Homiletics, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### vv. 9–10: Sons by Hodesh

- Seven sons are listed from Shaharaim's wife **Hodesh**: Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcham (or Malcam), Jeuz, Shachia/Sakia, and Mirmah. They became "heads of families." (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- Ellicott observes that Mesha and Malcham have a distinctly **Moabite cast**: Mesha shares the name of the famous Moabite king (2 Kings 3:4), and Malcham echoes Milcom, the god of Moab and Ammon (Jeremiah 49:1). This points to the cultural and religious influence of the Moabite environment. (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### v. 11: "He also had sons by Hushim: Abitub and Elpaal."

- These two sons by **Hushim** were born before she was sent away/divorced (v. 8). In clan terms, they represent two offshoots that did **not** participate in the emigration to Moab, but remained settled near Lod/Lydda. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm); Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Elpaal** becomes the patriarch of a large number of descendants traced in vv. 12–28.

### v. 12: "The sons of Elpaal: Eber, Misham, Shemed (who built Ono and Lod with its villages)..."

- **Shemed** (or Shamed/Shamer) **built Ono and Lod**. The Talmud states these were walled cities from the days of Joshua that were destroyed in the days of the concubine at Gibeah (Judges 19–20), and Elpaal (or Shemed) rebuilt them. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Lod** is the **Lydda** of Acts 9:32 (where Peter healed Aeneas); it is the modern village of Ludd, between Jaffa and Jerusalem. **Ono** is modern Kefr Auna, always coupled with Lod (Ezra 2:33; Nehemiah 7:37). (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm); Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Pulpit Homiletics** draws a lesson: "Human activity may have very long results. Shamed, the son of Elpaal, built two cities… Here we have an instance of the results of one man's activity being witnessed more than thirty centuries after he has been gathered to his fathers." (Pulpit Homiletics, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### v. 13: "...Beriah and Shema...who drove out the inhabitants of Gath."

- **Beriah and Shema** were heads of the clans inhabiting **Aijalon** (originally assigned to Dan, Joshua 19:42). They **drove away the inhabitants of Gath**, presumably in revenge for what the men of Gath had done to the Ephraimites (1 Chr 7:21). (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm); Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Pulpit Homiletics** draws a moral: "Violence is a bad foundation of rest and power… In the previous chapter we read that the inhabitants of Gath slew the sons of Ephraim. Truly 'they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.'" (Pulpit Homiletics, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary adds: "Hence retribution certain." (Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-chronicles-8.html))

### vv. 14–16: The sons of Beriah

- Nine sons of Beriah are listed: Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, Arad, Eder, Michael, Ishpah, and Joha. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### vv. 17–18: The sons of Elpaal

- Seven sons of Elpaal: Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki/Hezeki, Heber, Ishmerai, Izliah/Jezliah, and Jobab. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm); Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### vv. 19–21: The sons of Shimei

- Nine sons of **Shimei** (the same as Shema, brother of Beriah and son of Elpaal, v. 13): Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel, Adaiah, Beraiah, and Shimrath. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### vv. 22–25: The sons of Shashak

- Eleven sons of **Shashak** (another son of Elpaal, v. 14): Ishpan, Eber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah, Iphdeiah, and Penuel. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### vv. 26–27: The sons of Jeroham

- Six sons of **Jeroham** (probably the same as Jeremoth of v. 14, another son of Elpaal): Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah, Jaareshiah, Elijah, and Zichri. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Kimchi**, a medieval Jewish commentator, records a tradition that **Elijah** here is Elijah the prophet, who was of the seed of Rachel (Benjamin's mother). Gill notes this without endorsing it. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### v. 28: "All these were heads of families, the chiefs according to their genealogies, and they lived in Jerusalem."

- This sums up all the names from v. 14 to v. 27 — the descendants of Elpaal and their sons. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- Part of Jerusalem lay within Benjamin's tribal territory (Joshua 18:28; 15:63). However, "we do not hear of Benjamites inhabiting it until return from Captivity" (1 Chr 9:13; Nehemiah 11:4). (Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-chronicles-8.html))
- Ellicott notes this statement contrasts the five branches of Benjamin dwelling in Jerusalem with those clans that dwelt in Geba and Manahath (v. 6), in Moab (vv. 9–10), in Lod and Ono (v. 12), and in Aijalon (v. 13). (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Benson's Commentary** says: "Particular notice is taken of these, that others, at their return from captivity, might be induced to settle there too, which it seems few were willing to do, because it was the post of danger." (Benson, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-chronicles-8.html))
- **Pulpit Homiletics** draws a lesson from this: "The thought of a worthy ancestry is an honourable inducement to well-doing… The fact that their ancestors dwelt in the city would probably operate as a powerful inducement to lead many to offer themselves as citizens." (Pulpit Homiletics, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### v. 29: "Jeiel the father of Gibeon lived in Gibeon. His wife's name was Maacah."

- **"Father of Gibeon"** means the chief or ruler of the Benjamites dwelling there. His actual name, **Jehiel**, has accidentally dropped out of this verse but is supplied in the parallel passage, 1 Chronicles 9:35. (Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm); Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Gibeon** (modern el-Jib, about eight miles northwest of Jerusalem) was an important religious centre where the central sanctuary stood during most of Saul's reign until Solomon built the temple. However, Constable notes that the ark was never in the sanctuary at Gibeon — Gibeon was "the people's choice, even as Saul was. God's choice was Jerusalem." (Constable, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-8.html))

### vv. 30–32: The sons of Jeiel (the father of Gibeon)

- **Abdon** firstborn, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zecher/Zacher. Two names are missing from this list compared to the parallel in 1 Chronicles 9:36–37: **Ner** (after Baal) and **Mikloth** (after Zecher). Both missing names, however, appear in the verses that follow. (Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- The name **Baal** is noteworthy. Ellicott observes that the title "Baal" (meaning "Lord") was once applied to Jehovah in common speech (see Hosea 2:16: "Thou shalt call me Ishi, and shalt no more call me Baali"). After the name became associated with idolatrous cults, it was discarded in favour of Adonai. (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Mikloth** was father of **Shimeah** (called Shimeam in 1 Chr 9:38). "These also lived alongside their relatives in Jerusalem" — that is, of all the stock of Gibeon, only the branch of Mikloth-Shimeah settled in Jerusalem, living "over against" (east of) their brethren in Gibeon. (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm); Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### v. 33: "Ner was the father of Kish, Kish was the father of Saul..."

- This is the pivotal verse — **the royal house of Saul**. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- In 1 Samuel 9:1, Kish is said to be "son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Bechorath, son of Aphiah." **Ner** here, Gill notes, is also called Abiel (per the Targum); "Ner had two names, as other Jewish writers likewise say." (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- Saul's four sons named here: **Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Esh-baal**. Saul actually had nine children in total — also Ishui (1 Sam 14:49), two daughters Merab and Michal (1 Sam 14:49), and two sons by Rizpah, Armoni and Mephibosheth (2 Sam 21:8). (Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Esh-baal** ("man of Baal") is the **Ish-bosheth** ("man of shame") of 2 Samuel 2:8. The Cambridge Bible explains that "Baal" (Lord) was applied in early days to the national God of Israel (so to Saul and Samuel, Eshbaal meant "Man of the Lord," i.e., of Jehovah), but later prophets objected because it was applied to heathen gods. The author/reviser of Samuel therefore changed the offensive "Baal" to "Bosheth" ("shame"). The Chronicler, using a less-read text, preserved the original form. (Cambridge Bible, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Pulpit Homiletics**: "It is wise to stamp bad things with an evil name… Thus, by a simple name, the heathen deity was branded with public reprobation. The evil thing was made to seem the ugly and offensive thing it was." (Pulpit Homiletics, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Abinadab** appears as Ishui in 1 Samuel 14:49 — a case of double naming. (Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### v. 34: "The son of Jonathan: Merib-baal, and Merib-baal was the father of Micah."

- **Merib-baal** ("Baal strives" or "Man of Baal") is the **Mephibosheth** of 2 Samuel 4:4 and 9:6. The same substitution of "bosheth" (shame) for "baal" occurred here. (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm); Cambridge Bible, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Micah** is called Jonathan's "young son" in David's time (2 Sam 9:12). He is the great-grandson of Saul. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm); Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### v. 35: "The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz."

- **Tarea** is called **Tahrea** in the parallel passage 1 Chronicles 9:41 — a harder pronunciation of the same name. (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm); Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### v. 36: "Ahaz was the father of Jehoaddah..."

- **Jehoaddah** appears as **Jarah** in 1 Chronicles 9:42 — likely a scribal error arising from the common confusion of the Hebrew letters *d* and *r*. The name should probably be read "Jo'addah," a contraction. (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Zimri**: The Pulpit Commentary notes it is possible that this Zimri may rightly be identified with the usurper Zimri of 1 Kings 16:9–20, though this is uncertain. (Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Alemeth** is also the name of a Levitical town (1 Chr 6:60) and a son of Becher (1 Chr 7:8). (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))

### vv. 37–38: From Moza to Azel

- **Rapha** appears as **Rephaiah** in 1 Chronicles 9:43. (Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Azel** had six sons. Some manuscripts read "his firstborn" instead of **Bocheru** (which would be an anomalous proper name). The LXX and Syriac support this reading. (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- Adam Clarke (quoted in Enduring Word/Guzik) records that R.S. Jarchi (a medieval Jewish commentator) said "their allegorical expositions were sufficient to load thirteen thousand camels!" Clarke calls this "a shameful hyperbole." (Enduring Word/Guzik, [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-4-8/))

### vv. 39–40: Eshek, Ulam, and the 150 archers

- **Eshek** was the brother of Azel. Little is known of him. The genealogy of the house of Saul probably extends here to the time of Hezekiah (Ulam being the twelfth generation from Saul, as Hezekiah was the thirteenth from David). (Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-chronicles-8.html); Pulpit, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Ulam's sons** were "mighty men of valor, archers" — literally "treaders of the bow," meaning they drew large bows by bracing them with the foot. The Benjaminites were famous for their prowess: left-handed slingers in Judges 20, and archers here. (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- They had **150** sons and grandsons. Ellicott suggests this number is consistent with a family of the period of the Return from exile (cf. Ezra 2 for families of similar size that returned with Zerubbabel). Some Vulgate manuscripts read 150,000 — likely a corruption. (Ellicott, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/8.htm); Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** notes that the Benjaminites' boldness and cunning (Jacob's prophecy of Benjamin as a "wolf," Genesis 49:27) were "turned to spiritual good in Saul of Tarsus who became Paul the Apostle" (cf. Philippians 3:1–9). (Garner-Howes, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-chronicles-8.html))
- "All these are of the sons of Benjamin" — the chapter thus closes the genealogy of Benjamin with this summary statement. (Gill, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/8.htm))

---

## Distinctive Protestant Readings

### Reformed / Broader Evangelical (Constable, Payne, Wilcock)

- **Constable** (Dallas Theological Seminary) stresses that the Chronicler's genealogies function as a **sermon**. Chapters 8–9 prepare for Saul's death in chapter 10. The contrast between Gibeon (Saul's sanctuary, the people's choice) and Jerusalem (God's choice, David's city) is a major theological theme: "God permitted leadership by Saul and worship at Gibeon, but His plan called for leadership by David and worship at Jerusalem. Thus the Chronicler reminded his readers that their forefathers' premature insistence that God give them a king like all the other nations was a serious mistake." (Constable, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-8.html))

### Baptist (Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary)

- Emphasises Benjamin's martial character as **fulfilment of Jacob's prophecy** (Genesis 49:27) and sees a typological connection to Saul of Tarsus (Paul), in whom these traits were turned to spiritual zeal. (Garner-Howes, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-chronicles-8.html))

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik)

- David Guzik (Enduring Word) draws attention to the **post-exilic context**: "most of these settlements were in the area of Jerusalem, which was the main area that the returning exiles came to in the days when Chronicles was written." He quotes Payne: "Chronicles elaborates this material… primarily because of the importance of Benjamin as a tribe, which ranked second only to Judah in postexilic society." Guzik also notes Adam Clarke's caution about allegorising: "May they never recover their footing!" (Enduring Word, [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-4-8/))

### Methodist (Benson's Commentary)

- **Benson** emphasises the **practical application** for the returned exiles: the Benjamites who dwelt in Jerusalem are noted so that others "at their return from captivity, might be induced to settle there too, which it seems few were willing to do, because it was the post of danger." The names of the Israel of God are "carefully preserved in everlasting remembrance: a figure of God's writing the names of his spiritual Israel in the Lamb's book of life." (Benson, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-chronicles-8.html))

### G. Campbell Morgan (Congregational / Evangelical)

- Morgan sees the chapter as leading up to David: "the chief interest of the Book centers around David, and everything is made to lead up to him… Saul was his implacable foe, Jonathan his choicest friend. The love of the latter very largely compensated for the cruelty of the former." (Morgan, [studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gcm/1-chronicles-8.html))

### Esh-baal / Merib-baal Naming (Common to All Traditions)

- The substitution of "Bosheth" ("shame") for "Baal" in the books of Samuel — while Chronicles preserves the original "Baal" — is universally noted across all traditions. The Cambridge Bible explains this clearly: in Saul's day, "Baal" simply meant "Lord" and could refer to Yahweh, but later prophets objected. The less-publicly-read Chronicles preserved the uncensored names. (Cambridge Bible, [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/1_chronicles/8.htm))
